newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Steel cuts take Australia's Newcastle back to coal.
newsitem.headline: Steel cuts take Australia's Newcastle back to coal.

text.p: Newcastle, an Australian industrial city named after its English cousin, sacrificed thousands of jobs in the 1980s to save its old steel works, only to be told on Tuesday that the plant was closing anyway.

The closure is a big retreat for Australia. The Broken Hill Proprietary Co Ltd (BHP) plant, at the foot of the coal-rich Hunter Valley, was opened in World War One as the first major step towards downstream processing of the continent's vast mineral resources.

Like northern England and dozens of other industrial centres around the world, Newcastle drove hard in the 1980s to increase efficiency. Steel jobs fell from 12,000 to just 3,000, and the plant's enormous car parks became largely empty even at the change of shifts.

But while jobs were slashed, BHP left the mill unmodernised and the company declared on Tuesday the increasingly competitive world steel market would force it to shut down the 82-year-old plant by 1999 rather than overhaul it.

"To lose such a chunk of steelmaking capacity is tragic, not just for the workers but for this country and its capacity to make things," New South Wales state Premier Bob Carr told reporters after the announcement.

Newcastle's 470,000 people, unlike their English counterparts, can fall back on a mighty coal export industry -- huge mines, two-km (1.3-mile) long trains, the world's largest coal loader and a daily parade of giant ships tug in and out of the city's sunny harbour.
But the 1980s job losses in steel and other industries have already driven unemployment in the city over 12 percent, and it can now only go higher.
A thoroughly working class city in an unusually egalitarian country, Newcastle has suffered more than its fair share of hard knocks in recent years.
A 1989 earthquake which killed 13 people was as great a shock to the population as to the buildings, because earthquakes are almost unknown in Australia, and damage was extensive.
Months before, it had suffered the dispiriting loss of a crucial contract to build a new fleet of warships, which could have revived a shipbuilding past that had largely disappeared in the 1970s.
Locals are amazed that Australia is retreating from steel.

The continent has seemingly inexhaustible reserves of iron ore and high quality coal, but finds itself sending these bulk commodities overseas for the Japanese and South Koreans to turn into steel, which they use to build such products as cars that they export back to Australia.
"Nowhere in BHP's statement are they talking about new technology and that is a tragedy," said Newcastle MP Alan Morris, who has repeatedly called for investment rather than retreat.

"I call on the prime minister (John Howard) to intervene directly in this matter in the national interest, with a view to encouraging if not BHP then other prospective steelmakers to become active as quickly as possible, otherwise we will see a total loss of steelmaking in this country within 15 years."

BHP operates three full-scale steel plants in Australia -- Newcastle (with a capacity of two million tonnes a year), Port Kembla in the New South Wales city of Wollongong (five million tonnes) and Whyalla in South Australia (1.2 million tonnes).
